entities.summary:
King Wu of Zhou, personal name Ji Fa, was the founding king of the Chinese Zhou dynasty. The chronology of his reign is disputed but is generally thought to have begun around 1046 BC and ended with his death three years later. King Wu's military campaigns extended from modern-day Beijing to the city of Xianyang, in what is now northwest China. His victories over the neighboring tribes and the Eastern Zhou state cemented his legacy as a skilled military leader and a unifier of the Chinese state.





King Wu's reforms aimed to strengthen the Zhou dynasty's institutions and economy. He established the system of 'du' (feudal lordships) to govern the state's territories and created the 'yi' (official) to serve as administrators. These reforms also included the creation of a standardized system of weights and measures, as well as a common calendar.





King Wu's personal life is shrouded in mystery, but it is known that he had multiple wives and concubines. He also had a number of children, including a son named King Wu Ding, who succeeded him as ruler.





The legacy of King Wu of Zhou has endured for centuries, with his military campaigns and reforms continuing to be studied by historians and military strategists alike.

King Wu of Zhou's reign was marked by significant cultural achievements, including the development of a standardized system of writing, known as Oracle Bones, which was used for divination and record-keeping. The Zhou dynasty also saw the rise of Confucianism, which would go on to become one of the dominant philosophical schools in Chinese history.
